title: Trump backs Pete Hegseth amid renewed tensions with Iran – live
summary: Trump said he thinks his defense secretary ‘has done a great job’
body: The US Senate voted ⁠51 to 43 on Monday to advance the nomination of Walter “Jay” Clayton to serve as the next director of national intelligence. Despite a lack of prior intelligence experience, which is mandated by law, Clayton is Donald Trump’s pick to replace Tulsi Gabbard in the role, which is being held on an acting basis by another political ally of the president, Bill Pulte, who also lacked that qualification when he took up the post last month. Donald Trump wrapped up remarks at the General Motors Proving Ground in Milford, Michigan a short time ago with a pair of lies he has repeated many, many times. The first was his claim that “mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt” and the only reason for anyone to oppose his drive to require proof of citizenship to register to vote, and photo ID to cast a ballot, is that his opponents want to cheat. “We want voter photo ID. And we want all voters showing proof of a thing called citizenship,” Trump said late in his speech. “You read recently in New Jersey, where tremendous numbers of people were found out that they were on the voter rolls totally illegally, and that’s all over the country,” he added, mischaracterizing the scale of a computer glitch in New Jersey’s automatic voter registration system for licensed drivers that mistakenly registered about 6,600 people who identified themselves as non-US citizens. According to the state’s governor, Mikie Sherrill, who last week revealed the software error that was corrected before the 2024 election, “fewer than 400 individuals who were newly registered for the first time because of the error voted,” and they were registered as Republicans, Democrats and Independents. “While administrative errors such as New Jersey’s do infrequently occur, they are very rare and affect a very small fraction of voters, David Becker, a voting rights expert who leads the nonprofit Center for Election Innovation & Research said. “In this case, the number of wrongful registrations represents a miniscule fraction, roughly 0.1%, of New Jersey’s total active voter registration records in 2024.” The president went on to claim that even he had been asked for ID when he voted at some unspecified time in the past. “Even me, I went to vote. ‘Sir, may I please see your identification? Sir, I’m so embarrassed; I know you’re Trump. Please. Do you have some identification? I don’t want to lose my job.’ I whipped out- I was lucky I had some kind of a card on me, I didn’t even know, but I gave it.” Trump did not say when this exchange took place, but he reportedly voted by mail himself earlier this year in a March special election in Florida even though he was in Palm Beach on the day the ballot was requested and returned. Trump did vote in person in Palm Beach in the 2024 and 2020 general elections, but his fuzzy memory about what sort of “a card” he provided as ID when asked at the polls suggests that it could have been a debit card, which was a sort of non-photo ID acceptable at the time to vote, along with other cards, like student IDs or retirement center IDs, that Florida poll workers could accept before the state’s law changed this year. Under the new law none of those forms of ID will be accepted any longer, requiring voters to produce a new form of drivers’ license that confirms citizenship, or a passport or a birth certificate along with another form of photo ID. While Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on voting rights advocates who oppose proof of citizenship and photo ID to register and cast ballots, a 2023 survey by the Brennan Center suggested that “more than 9 percent of American citizens of voting age, or 21.3 million people, don’t have proof of citizenship readily available”, meaning a passport, birth certificate, or naturalization papers. “And at least 3.8 million don’t have these documents at all, often because they were lost, destroyed, or stolen.” The Center for Democracy and Civic Engagement at the University of Maryland reported in 2024 that nearly 21 million voting-age US citizens “do not have a current (non-expired) driver’s license” and another 28.6 million have a non-expired license, but it does not have both their current address and current name. Before leaving Michigan, Trump also repeated a tale he has been telling for a decade, despite the fact that it is not true: that he was named Michigan’s Man of the Year before he ran for president. “I was here 25 years ago. I got Man of the Year,” Trump said, as he has claimed in the past during visits to the state as president. “The press questioned that and then they found out it was true, actually,” he added, falsely. As CNN’s tireless fact-checker Daniel Dale reported in 2024, the origin of Trump’s claim appears to be that he was invited to speak at a Republican event in the state in 2013, where, according to a former Republican congressman who was there, Trump was presented with a framed copy of Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address. Years later, when Trump started claiming he had been given a Michigan Man of the Year award, the congressman told CNN that was untrue. But a local Republican group tied to make it seem true in 2023, by naming Trump the state’s Man of the Decade. The Trump administration has asked the US supreme court to allow implementation nationwide of his executive order aimed at tightening rules ⁠for mail-in voting ahead of the ⁠November midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. In a filing, the justice department requested that the justices put on hold a judge’s ruling preventing the enforcement of the president’s directive in 23 mostly Democratic-governed ⁠states and Washington DC, which had challenged the order as unconstitutional, while the litigation plays out. Last month, US district judge Indira ⁠Talwani ruled that the provisions of an executive order issued by Donald Trump on 31 March requiring the postal service to require the use of a barcode tracking system for ballot envelopes tied to US Citizenship and Immigration Services data was unconstitutional. It comes amid Trump’s wider drive to reshape rules and regulations around voting ahead of the midterms. Trump is pushing Congress to pass the Save America Act, which would impose new ID requirements on voters and curtail mail-in voting, which he has long railed against alleging widespread fraud – despite never producing any evidence of this and despite the fact the he has voted by mail himself. Donald Trump has told the crowd at General Motors Proving Grounds in Milford, Michigan, that the US has been ⁠having “very friendly” talks with Iran. You ⁠can’t bribe them. You’ve ‌got ‌to beat them, ‌and we’ll beat the hell out of them. But we’ll ‌see how it turns out. Right now, ⁠there are very friendly negotiations going on. Former FBI director James Comey urged a judge today to throw out federal charges against him, arguing that a photo of seashells arranged on a beach he posted on social media was not a call to violence against Donald Trump but protected political speech. Comey’s lawyers argue the government cannot prove the photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47” constituted a “true threat” against the president, who fired Comey in 2017 and has publicly called for his prosecution. The slogan has long meant to “get rid of” or “eject”, and Trump is the 47th president. The justice department previously tried and failed to bring a separate case against Comey. After that federal prosecutors focused on the 2025 social media post featuring the seashells spelling out “86 47”. Comeuy captioned the post: “Cool shell formation on my beach walk.” “But the government now singles out Mr Comey to prosecute one of the President’s most prominent critics for publishing another person’s statement of political opposition,” his attorney’s wrote. “That attempt to suppress core political speech contravenes both the statutes at issue and the First Amendment.” Comey’s attorneys argued that to be a “true threat” under the law, his post would have needed to communicate a “serious expression” that he was going to commit violence. “No reasonable observer who was aware of the relevant context would read the phrase ‘86 47’ to connote violence against the President,” Comey’s attorneys wrote. “But even if ‘86 47’ could implausibly be read to suggest violence, a reasonable observer would still understand Mr Comey’s post as mere political hyperbole, not a true threat.” The justice department has not elaborated on any evidence of intent the government has. The case is due to go to trial in October. Donald Trump is speaking now at General Motors Proving Grounds in Milford, Michigan. I’ll bring you all the key lines from his remarks here. title: DNC chair faces growing scrutiny amid financial pressure and internal turmoil
summary: Fraught time for Ken Martin as new reporting details cash-flow problem and divisions over party’s direction
body: Mounting financial pressures and growing internal turmoil at the Democratic National Committee (DNC) have intensified scrutiny of chair Ken Martin, as new reporting detailed a deepening cash-flow problem, management concerns and widening divisions over the party’s direction less than 100 days before the November midterm elections. The latest reporting has underscored both the committee’s financial distress and the toll it has taken on Martin personally. The New York Times reported that the embattled DNC chair, who took the helm last year, became the subject of an internal HR inquiry after throwing his phone in the direction of a junior aide’s desk during a heated exchange in early July, prompting a formal complaint. The Times, citing people familiar with the matter, also reported that the incident nearly cost him his job and has contributed to growing isolation with the party as the committee grapples with mounting financial strain. The latest revelations include that the DNC put its physical Washington DC headquarters up for collateral last year in order to obtain a $15m line of credit to help invest in off-year elections, Notus reported, citing Washington DC deed records. The New York Times separately reported that the DNC is about $2m in debt, compared with roughly $130m cash on hand held by the Republican National Committee. The committee argued that the arrangement was “not new” and that it had done so to secure loans previously. However, one DNC member told the outlet: “Ken is gaslighting us about the DNC’s finances and not being transparent about the financial situation makes us doubt if he can oversee the DNC during the most important primary of our lifetime.” Another Democrat close to Martin told Notus he had struggled to convince donors to maximize their contributions, which had contributed to the small cash-on-hand total. Adding to the party’s financial woes, the Times reported that the DNC had asked vendors not to send invoices until after the midterm elections in November. Roger Lau, the executive director of the DNC, told the Times in a statement that the bill-deferral discussions were “nothing more than standard negotiations with vendors over contracts and payment processes”. It’s an increasingly fraught time for Martin, whose tenure has been marked by turbulence almost since the start, when he became embroiled in a public spat with then vice-chair David Hogg. Their philosophical disagreement proved irreconcilable and Hogg eventually quit. Faith in Martin’s leadership had eroded further following his botched handling of a long-promised autopsy of the 2024 election that ultimately failed to address what actually went wrong for the party – from Gaza to the Biden-Harris transition. The release in May prompted a round of calls for Martin’s resignation. Last week, Martin defended the state of the DNC’s finances in an op-ed on Substack, writing that the committee had made the “conscious decision” to spend the cash it raises on “electoral assets” rather than stockpiling resources. He said the DNC had “done exceptionally better with high-net worth donors”, citing an increase of donations from major donors relative to comparable years. “We must measure success by power built, not simply dollars retained,” he added. But some veteran Democratic fundraisers remain unconvinced. In a Substack essay published on Monday, former Democratic finance chair and former US ambassador Rufus Gifford argued the party’s financial problems stem from a broader collapse in donor confidence. “I think there is no saving Martin’s chairmanship,” Gifford wrote, arguing that the “two main jobs” of the DNC chair were to “raise money and message relentlessly on every form of media”. The committee, he warned, was at risk of becoming “irrelevant” unless it found a way to restore donor trust and rebuild its national fundraising operation before the 2028 presidential campaign. The reports renewed calls for Martin to step aside, which he has firmly resisted. “Ken Martin must resign,” Congressman Sam Liccardo, a California Democrat, wrote on X. “As Democrats, we have become too captured by failing strategies. We must fail forward, and pivot. The urgency of this moment will not reward – and our children will not forgive – torpidity.” But at a campaign event in Pennsylvania on Sunday, Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, expressed confidence in Martin, telling reporters covering the rally that the DNC chair had his “full support”.

title: France and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave begins
summary: Coming days are ‘absolutely critical’ for firefighters before temperatures rise again this week, officials say
body: Firefighters in France and Spain are racing to bring huge wildfires under control before another heatwave this week that will complicate efforts to tame the flames. Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said Monday and Tuesday were “absolutely crucial days” before temperatures rise again from Wednesday. EU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year for the area of land burned. A fire in the hilly terrain of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become Spain’s largest on record, burning 50,000 hectares (125,000 acres). Authorities are battling two separate fires north-west of Madrid, taking the total area of scorched land near the capital to 70,000 hectares. France was also in “a race against time” to control wildfires before another heatwave this week, said Eric Brocardi, a fire service spokesperson. Weather forecasters have said temperatures could reach 40C (104F) is some parts of the country from Tuesday. This would complicate efforts to control the wildfire in Gironde in south-west France, which the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as “extremely intense and unpredictable … generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area”. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, on a visit to Bordeaux, said: “The coming weeks will be tough and we have to hold out.” But he said a smaller fire in the adjoining Landes – which forced the evacuation of more than 30,000 people – was “contained” but remained “virulent”. “We must be extremely cautious over the next few hours and the coming days,” he said. The Gironde fire has so far burned 42,000 hectares, making it one of the biggest devastations of land in France since the second world war. In the Cestas commune, about 10 miles from the city of Bordeaux, firefighters used mechanical diggers to uproot trees in an attempt to create a firebreak. The vast fire, which has triggered the evacuation of 220,000 people, had not progressed during the early hours of Monday but was “not contained” and remained “very complicated to control”, Nuñez said. Speaking after an emergency meeting of the French government on Monday, he described this year’s wildfires as “completely exceptional”. More than 116,000 hectares of forest and vegetation have been burned since January, far exceeding the 70,000 hectares reported for the whole of 2025. Spain’s government said the 172,000 hectares of forested land burned this year was six times greater than the equivalent figure for 2025. The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, told a climate conference the wildfires were not isolated incidents. “It is the most painful manifestation of a climate emergency that is making … wildfires more voracious and heatwaves more frequent, and as a result our land more vulnerable,” he said. “It is no longer an exception. It is the rule.” The European Commission’s lead official on the green transition, Teresa Ribera, said Europe was not prepared for the consequences of the climate crisis. In an interview with El País she said the commission would propose an adaptation strategy in October that would be much more comprehensive than policies implemented so far. A series of heatwaves, including record-breaking temperatures in June, that scientists say would have been impossible without the climate crisis, has left parched soils and tinder-dry vegetation that have fuelled this summer’s fires. A European Commission official said the wildfire season had begun in April and could last until early November. Officials also stressed the rising risks for fighting wildfires from the middle of the week in France, Spain and Greece. The EU executive has coordinated the dispatch of seven planes and four helicopters to France, as well as six planes and three forest firefighting teams to Spain, after the countries triggered the bloc’s emergency assistance mechanism. EU officials have also been sent to the Bordeaux region to assist local authorities. Officials stressed the unprecedented nature of recent fires, which have spread rapidly over large areas. A commission official said that a recent fire in southern Spain that killed 13 people had reached speeds of 4 mph, while firefighters are able to react only to fires moving 300 metres an hour or less. The scale of Europe’s wildfires has raised questions about the continent’s ability to respond. Italy is among about 10 European countries that have sent firefighting equipment or teams to France and Spain while grappling with its own blazes. Firefighters fought to extinguish a major wildfire in Italy’s southern region of Puglia on Monday. More than 400 people, many of them tourists staying in campsites set among pine forests, were evacuated by sea from the Gargano peninsula on Sunday as the blaze, fanned by strong winds, encroached on beaches. A further 58 people were evacuated from their homes in Maratea as a wildfire swept through neighbouring Basilicata. Italy is bracing for its fourth heatwave this year as temperatures edge up towards highs of 38C to 40C from Wednesday. Smoke from the fires in France is continuing to cause a “marked deterioration” in air quality across a swathe of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region and beyond, with health authorities warning about the danger. Elderly people, pregnant women and those with respiratory issues and chronic conditions were advised to take precautions. Local health authorities said people should close windows, wear an FFP2 mask outside and avoid strenuous activity. The prime minister’s office said more than 1.5 million FFP2 masks had been sent to the region.

title: Trump warns of return to ‘strong military action’ if Iran diplomacy fails
summary: Washington and Tehran issue conflicting messages over the status of talks to end Middle East crisis
body: Donald Trump has once again warned that the US will return to “strong military action” against Iran if diplomatic efforts do not bring a rapid resolution to the crisis in the Middle East. “We are in very deep talks with Iran. If they don’t work out, we will go back to very strong military action,” the US president told Axios on Monday. Asked for how long he would allow the talks to proceed, he answered: “Not much time. Either it goes fast or not at all.” He reiterated the line to reporters later the same day on Air Force One. “They want to meet, and we’re meeting. Without what we did, they wouldn’t even be talking to us … They would not have requested the meeting if we were doing poorly. The only reason they want to meet is because we’ve been hitting them very hard.” He doubled down at a rally in Michigan soon after. “You ⁠can’t bribe them. You’ve ‌got ‌to beat them, ‌and we’ll beat the hell out of them. But we’ll ‌see how it turns out,” he said . “Right now, ⁠there are very friendly negotiations going on.” Earlier, Tehran said there were no direct talks with the US to end the conflict, which began in late February with a wave of US-Israeli strikes and has rocked the region and the global economy. “Mediators may convey messages from the American side to us regarding current developments in the region. But at present we are not engaged in any negotiations with the United States,” said the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei. The diplomatic back and forth came as Oman and Iran drew closer to an agreement in principle on the future management of the strait of Hormuz, but remained unable to resolve Tehran’s demand that all ships passing through the strategic waterway must pay some type of transit fee or toll to a consortium led by the two countries. Oman and Iran met for technical talks in Tehran on Friday and Saturday that may hold the key to preventing a further round of fighting. Perceived progress in the talks – backed by China, Qatar and Pakistan – was understood to have fed into the US decision to pause its attacks on Iran after nearly two weeks. Senior US officials are also reported to have warned Trump over dwindling US munitions stockpiles and the impact of Iranian reprisals on US bases in the region, including Kuwait and Jordan. The top US military commander in the Middle East, Adm Brad Cooper, reportedly recommended stopping the bombing campaign around the strait because it had reached the limit of its effectiveness. The US attacks have been described by Washington as a response to repeated Iranian breaches of the memorandum of understanding signed in June, including by trying to prevent commercial shipping from transiting the strait through a southern route overseen by the US. Iran argues the southern route breaks the ceasefire agreement, which it insists left the country in sole charge of how the strait was reopened. A diplomat said: “The aim of the Tehran talks is to marry the Iran and Oman proposals so what emerges is clearly compliant with the law of the sea, and internationally acceptable.” At a Tehran press conference, Baqaei denied that the pause in US fighting amounted to an informal ceasefire. Oman has been trying since May to persuade Tehran that any plan for charging fees in the strait must be voluntary, to comply with the law of the sea. It has proposed a model similar to that which governs the strait of Malacca: countries that use it voluntarily contribute to a fund that provides for environmental and safety services to shipping. Oman argues that a similar entity could be set up in the strait of Hormuz with the agreement of the UN and the International Maritime Organization. The IMO secretary general, Arsenio Dominguez, has told the Guardian that the Malacca strait model is worth considering for the strait of Hormuz. Iran’s department of environment has drafted its own plan, under which “the annual passage of over 50,000 ships and oil tankers through the strait of Hormuz and their role in polluting the Persian Gulf” must be compensated for. Under the plan, Iran would be able to collect “fees” from passing vessels proportional to the type of ship, cargo volume, navigation history and history of pollution. The comparison between the straits of Malacca and Hormuz is imperfect since fewer ships see ports in the Malacca strait as a destination point. But the Iranian media appear increasingly drawn to the Malacca model. The Khabaronline news agency argued such an agreement would be “a win-win situation for Iran”. Baqaei described the talks with Oman as useful and constructive but said they had nothing to do with the US. “The goal is for Iran and Oman, as two coastal states, to develop mechanisms to ensure safe shipping in the strait of Hormuz, while respecting the sovereign rights of the two coastal states and also preserving Iran’s security and national interests,” he said. Oman is in a tight spot since it knows the US is opposed to the introduction of tolls, but it may accept a very clearly delineated system of fees for specific services. The talks come as the US continues to encourage commercial shipping to test the strength of the Iranian blockade of the strait. Iranian officials reported that six vessels with their navigation systems switched off attempted to pass through the southern route of the strait on Sunday. One of them was fired upon and the others were turned back to the Persian Gulf. The US has reimposed a blockade of Iranian oil exports and ended a sanctions waiver on its oil exports. The United Nations Office for Project Services said on Monday that transits through the strait of Hormuz had fallen to an average of approximately five ships a day over the past week, compared with nearly 130 a day before the war.

title: Trump administration’s revision of Iran war casualties ‘huge disrespect’, say veterans
summary: Defense department updated database of casualties to list four service members deceased in ‘Overseas Operations’
body: A controversial move by the Pentagon to reclassify casualties in the Iran war is being taken by US military veterans as a sign of disrespect for the dead. “It’s such a huge disrespect for the families,” said Michael E Smith, a retired US rear admiral and the founder of National Security Leaders for America. “To claim that they weren’t killed as a result of the war – oh, it was just overseas operations – is just ludicrous.” In a quiet weekend update to the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), a military database for displaying casualties, the US Department of Defense – renamed the Department of War under Donald Trump – added more than 140 wounded service members. They also introduced a new casualty category labeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7” which splits the count from the beginning of the US-Israel war on Iran. Four US service members killed in action by Iranian forces fall under that category: 1st Lt Tyler James Feehan, Pvt Isabella Gonzales, Sgt Angel S. Rampersad and Sgt Michael Emmanuel Swinton. “I definitely think that this isn’t an issue just about numbers, but also about accountability,” said Tristeza Ordex, a US Marine Corps veteran and the national organizer of partnerships and engagement at VoteVets. “When I was deployed to Afghanistan, I remember attending ramp ceremonies,” she said, referring to an airfield memorial honoring a fallen service member before their casket is loaded onto an aircraft and returned home. Gonzales, 19, was from Carrollton, Texas, near Ordex’ home near Dallas. Gonzales was not yet born when Ordex first enlisted in 2004. “Thinking about it now makes me emotional, to think about how we have people coming home now … 19 years old,” she said. “I think about people like her that were excluded. Not only are Latinos being excluded from so much more and being targeted: we have this person that paid the ultimate sacrifice for this country who isn’t even being recognized as a casualty of this war, so it feels like erasure.” The War Powers Act of 1973 requires the president to end military operations within 60 days unless Congress authorizes an extension, which it has not. The Trump administration has argued that the April ceasefire with Iran paused the clock on 1 May for the conflict’s initial period. The separate casualty count beginning on 7 July follows that interpretation. Smith, who completed combat tours in Iraq, Bosnia and Kosovo, likened the administrative change to the manipulation of Pentagon casualty data last seen in the Vietnam war. “It’s so disrespectful to our service members who gave their lives, and the only reason they died was because Donald Trump decided to do this illegal war,” Smith said. “I mean, clearly the president is very sensitive about the deaths. You know, he is comparing it to Korea and Vietnam. “Obviously their boss doesn’t want to hear about deaths. OK, well, here’s one way we can make it look like there’s not as many deaths.” The Pentagon was approached for comment. The department’s reclassification of Iran war casualties has faced criticism in Washington, including from Thomas Massie, a Republican House member from Kentucky, ousted in a primary earlier this year after repeatedly breaking with the president. “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire,” Massie wrote on X on Friday. “The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”. US senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, a Democrat on the armed services committee, added: “Americans deserve the truth about the human cost of President Trump’s Iran war, and I will not stop fighting until this administration gives our military members and their families the transparency and accountability they deserve.”

title: Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needs
summary: PM wants curriculums for students aged 14 and above to be more responsive to local jobs market
body: Andy Burnham will tell schools across England to adapt their curriculums to the needs of local businesses as part of a devolution drive aimed at tackling the jobs crisis for young people. By moving decision-making to local areas, the PM hopes the plan will make technical and vocational skills as valued as academic qualifications – and help cut the benefits bill. Based in part on the Greater Manchester baccalaureate that Burnham introduced as the region’s mayor, it will task schools with making their curriculums for students aged 14 and above more responsive to the local jobs market, teaching technical skills alongside traditional academic subjects. It would, Burnham said, mean the country could “value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap”. Described by No 10 as “a fundamental change to the education system”, the announcement kicks off a week of policy initiatives by Burnham, expected to also cover adult social care, defence and devolution. After last week’s succession of rapid, consumer-focused policies such as help with electricity bills, Burnham’s team aim to use the coming days to present him as a leader willing to tackle more intractable and complex political problems. Under the plan, intended to begin operating from September 2028, mayors and other local leaders would work with schools, colleges and employers to devise technical training built around local jobs. In combination, there will be prioritised funding for such technical and vocational qualifications, plus guidance to Ofsted to recognise the value of these as well as more traditional qualifications. In addition to giving local areas more control over education for the 14-16 age group, Burnham said the intention was to redress what he said was an over-simplified focus on academic routes. He said: “For too long in this country, students have been told that you must take the academic path to do well and to be respected. The whole school system has been built around it and that has let down young people seeking technical qualifications. “I want an education system based on parity between academic and technical which gives all young people a clear path in life. From today, Britain will value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap.” The intention is also to help address the worsening problem of young people not in education, employment or training, which was the subject of a report published in May by Alan Milburn, the former Labour cabinet minister. The first part of an ongoing review, Milburn’s report said the issue now affected 1 million young people across the UK, with the numbers rising fast. It cited a number of factors, including a changing job market, inequality and health problems, but also blamed a lack of focus on employability skills and non-academic qualifications. Milburn said in a statement that he welcomed the plans to overhaul and devolve education for 14-plus pupils, calling it “a big step in the right direction and consistent with the findings of my review”. Moves to get more young people into work will also be a key element of wider efforts to tackle the benefits system, due to be guided by both Milburn’s findings and a separate review by Stephen Timms, the minister for social security, into the personal independence payment disability system. In an interview with the BBC broadcast on Monday night, Burnham said he believed that many young people had been failed by a system that “pays for failure” rather than “sets people up for success”. Asked if he believed some people received benefits they did not need, he replied: “I wouldn’t necessarily go straight to blaming those people. What I would say is that there are people in the benefit system, young people in their 20s, who have been, I would say, quite seriously let down because the support wasn’t there for them when it should have been there.” This failure included, he said, “an education system that for a very long time has been obsessed on the university route but hasn’t done enough for young people who want technical qualifications and in many ways has treated them as second class students”. The new initiative is firmly based on Burnham’s flagship education policy as Greater Manchester mayor, introduced in September 2024. Known as the Greater Manchester baccalaureate, or MBacc, it was designed to offer courses and work experience for children aged 14 and over in key sectors in the regional economy. Alongside the traditional subjects of English, maths and sciences, schools in Greater Manchester can now offer technical lessons tailored towards employment in industries including financial services, engineering and manufacturing, construction and the green economy. There are also new routes into public services such as health and social care, education and transport. Experts say it is too soon to properly evaluate whether the MBacc has been a success – it was piloted in only 10 schools in its first academic year. However, several other of England’s regional mayors have called for greater power over the school curriculum to link it more closely with their local economy. Some mayors complain that the Department for Education has been one of the most stubborn government bodies when it comes to devolving powers outside Whitehall.

title: Police make inquiries after Farage reports Polanski post for ‘inciting murder’
summary: Green party leader shared picture of man wearing T-shirt with words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ alongside a guillotine
body: Police are “conducting inquiries” into an image shared by Green party leader Zack Polanski on Instagram after Reform UK reported it for “inciting murder”. The image showed a man wearing a black T-shirt with the words “we’re only making plans for Nigel”, alongside a photograph of a guillotine. A Green party spokesperson said that Polanski “condemns the image on the T-shirt” and accepted being tagged in a post with 20 images “without realising there was more to it than he had seen”. Nigel Farage shared a screenshot of the image on X and wrote: “This is what Zack Polanski has just posted on his Instagram. “If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski.” Reform UK’s spokesperson for home affairs, Zia Yusuf, said Polanski was “inciting murder”, and that sharing the image weeks after the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe, who was murdered in her home in Devon, was “staggering”. Last week, prosecutors told a court that a man allegedly hit Widdecombe 21 times over the head with a hammer in a “planned and targeted” attack. A Green party spokesperson said: “The T-shirt is clearly in poor taste, especially at a time of heightened fears for the security of public figures, having experienced multiple threats himself [Polanski]. “He [Polanski] and the Green party call on everyone involved in public discourse to show kindness and not encourage more division.” A spokesperson for the Metropolitan police said: “Earlier today, we received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media. “We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting inquiries into the matter.” Yusuf wrote on social media: “Zack Polanski has posted to his 713k Instagram followers a photo of a man in a T-shirt calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage. “Polanski is inciting murder. It must be treated as such by the police.” The image, which has since been removed from Polanski’s Instagram account, was shared in a collaborative post with other accounts, as part of a carousel of images from a Green party event on Sunday. The words on the T-shirt come from Making Plans for Nigel, a song by English rock band XTC, which was released as the lead single from the 1979 album Drums and Wires. A post on a website that appeared to sell the T-shirt for £20 stated: “Whether it’s a nod to old punk music or a sharper bit of political satire, this design is for those who prefer their statements with a side of mystery.” Earlier this month, Andy Burnham said that a serious review is needed into MP security after the murder of Ann Widdecombe. Jess Phillips previously told the Guardian that the threat to MPs must be tackled at source, amid an ongoing refusal by social media platforms to take responsibility for what’s published on their platforms. According to the BBC, Polanski has not been contacted by the police.

title: Man convicted in Idaho college student killings seeks to withdraw guilty plea
summary: Bryan Kohberger, convicted of killing four college students in 2022, claims he pleaded guilty due to bad legal advice
body: A man convicted last year of killing four college students in Idaho has filed to withdraw his guilty plea and seek a new trial, claiming he pleaded guilty due to bad legal advice. Bryan Kohberger was convicted of breaking into a six-bedroom house in 2022 and killing four University of Idaho students in their early 20s. The victims – Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin – were found dead with dozens of knife wounds. Goncalves also showed evidence of asphyxiation and blunt force trauma. “I hereby declare my intention to enter a not guilty plea, and welcome the State the opportunity to prove their case at trial, as well as to, again, file for the death penalty,” Kohberger wrote in a statement shared with the New York Times. “My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn.” Kohberger formally filed for post-conviction relief Monday in Ada county district court. According to the docket, Kohberger is representing himself. It is rare such serious convictions to be overturned after a guilty plea, though it is possible to challenge them on the basis of new evidence or negligent legal defense. Gonclaves’s family sharply criticized Kohberger’s attempt to challenge his conviction, describing him as a “narcissist” and “the mosquito you just can’t seem to swat.” “He chose not to leave his fate – or the facts of the case – to a jury,” reads the statement provided to KXLY. “He never cried foul, never claimed he was uninformed or pressured, and never suggested there were problems with the discovery materials he and his counsel had reviewed for two years that should have been challenged. He admitted his guilt.” “My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news,” Idaho attorney general Raúl Labrador said on social media. “My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out.” Kohberger, a former Washington State University doctoral student in criminal justice, is currently serving four consecutive life sentences without the opportunity for parole, along with an extra 10 years for a burglary conviction in the same case. No motive for the killings has ever been established or provided by Kohberger. Police found DNA matching Kohberger’s on a knife sheaf left at the murder scene. Surveillance video showed a white Hyundai Elantra like Kohberger’s passing multiple times around the house where the murders were committed. Kohberger’s cell phone was turned off at time the murders occurred. He was arrested the month after the murders in Pennsylvania, where he was visiting his father for the holidays in late December. On his person and in the Kohberger family home, investigators found a pistol, two knives, black gloves, a black hat and a black facemask. One of the survivors of the attack described witnessing a shadowy figure clad in black.

title: Andy Burnham appoints Bridget Phillipson as Labour party chair
summary: Former education secretary will take up influential role that puts her at vanguard of Labour’s battle to win next general election
body: Bridget Phillipson has been appointed Labour party chair, putting her at the vanguard of Labour’s battle to win the next general election. The former education secretary and architect of a landmark overhaul in special educational needs and disabilities (Send) provision in England will follow in the footsteps of other Labour big beasts who have held the position, including Harriet Harman, Angela Rayner and Tom Watson. Phillipson, who was sacked as education secretary by Andy Burnham last week, replaces Anna Turley after last week’s government reshuffle, which saw the Labour Co-op MP for Redcar moved to a new ministerial role in the Home Office. The prime minister said the MP for Houghton and Sunderland South would drive culture change and work alongside him and Lucy Powell. “She will play a vital role in ensuring the Labour party is match fit for the next election,” he said. “I am delighted Bridget has accepted this role and I look forward to working closely with her on this vital task.” After a major cabinet reshuffle in which dozens of cabinet ministers, including several loyal to Keir Starmer, were removed from their posts, Phillipson was viewed as a rare survivor, albeit in a reduced role. In what is likely to be seen as an olive branch to members of the previous government, Labour said the appointment reflected Burnham’s “commitment to drawing on the full breadth and depth of talent across the Labour party as he builds one united team”. Phillipson said she would put “Labour values and the voices of our movement at the heart of government”. She added: “By uniting together, we will bring hope back to communities and strengthen British society against those working to divide us.” Phillipson was demoted last week when she was replaced by key Burnham ally Powell as secretary of state for education. But she maintained her position in the cabinet as women and equalities minister, the first time the traditionally more minor role has been part of cabinet in its own right. While not an overt Burnhamite, the former education secretary was not seen as overly tribal and had won plaudits from Labour MPs for her engagement over plans to make provision for children with Send more widely available in mainstream schools. Critics raised concerns about the plans, which will raise the bar at which children in England qualify for an education, health and care plan (EHCP), which legally entitles them to get support. Phillipson has become something of a bete noire for some on the right after overseeing the Labour policy of applying 20% VAT to private school fees from the start of 2025, having recently been called a “spiteful class warrior” by Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch. Brought up in a low-income, single-parent household in the town of Washington, Tyne and Wear, Phillipson wrote a report on child poverty for Starmer and his chancellor Rachel Reeves, and argued that abolishing the two-child benefit cap was the most cost-effective way to make lives better for young disadvantaged people. She later told the BBC she was going to have Badenoch’s insult put on a T-shirt, adding: “If being a spiteful class warrior means lifting half a million children out of poverty I’ll be wearing that T-shirt with pride.” Having held the education brief since Labour entered government in July 2024, Phillipson was replaced by Powell, who became the 11th person to hold the post in the last decade. Powell, who is also deputy leader of the Labour party, has long been a Burnham ally. A fellow Manchester MP, she played a key role in helping win the Makerfield campaign, which saw him return to Westminster, and has previously run byelections as well as having directed Ed Miliband’s 2015 national Labour campaign.

title: US justice department dismisses charges against California union leader
summary: David Huerta was arrested while protesting against an ICE operation during crackdown in Los Angeles
body: The Department of Justice has moved to dismiss charges against a prominent California union leader who was arrested while protesting against an immigration raid in Los Angeles last year, in the latest US government case against protesters to fall apart. David Huerta, the president of Service Employees International Union United Service Workers West, was arrested at a June 2025 demonstration and has been fighting the charges ever since. On Monday, the US attorney’s office in LA filed a motion to dismiss the charges against him. Huerta was initially charged with “conspiracy to impede an officer”, a serious felony, though prosecutors earlier this year downgraded those charges to a misdemeanor of “obstruction, resistance, or opposition of a federal officer”. The misdemeanor is now on track for dismissal. The justice department in Los Angeles has aggressively prosecuted immigrants and protesters for “impeding” and “assaulting” immigration officers, but many of those cases have collapsed in court, with prosecutors facing a stunning streak of losses when the charges have gone to trial. “This means the government is finally admitting what we knew from day one and what was obvious to anyone who saw the videos: the charge against me was baseless, meant to intimidate anyone who dares to speak out, organize, or demand justice,” Huerta said in a statement on Monday. “There was never a real case, only an attempt to punish and silence me for exercising my constitutional rights.” The charges against Huerta stemmed from a 6 June 2025 protest against an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operation in LA’s garment district at the start of the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigrant communities in southern California. Huerta’s arrest was partially caught on camera, with footage showing him on the ground and agents on top of him during chaotic confrontations between officers and protesters. He was arrested and charged based on claims he was blocking a gate in front of a business’s warehouse where immigration agents were trying to make arrests. Huerta was hospitalized after his arrest, and his prosecution became one of the first high-profile criminal cases against a demonstrator objecting to ICE’s operations. The charges sparked widespread outrage, with the LA mayor, Karen Bass, criticizing the federal government for targeting “one of the most respected labor leaders in this country” and treating him “like a criminal”. Huerta’s union represents thousands of security officers, janitors, airport workers and other laborers across California. In his statement on Monday, Huerta said he had been “singled out” for “loudly” questioning agents’ actions during the raid, and he recalled officers tackling and pepper-spraying him before he was detained: “I consider myself fortunate to have been only detained, considering the murders in Minneapolis, Houston, Miami, and the deplorable conditions at federal detention centers throughout the country.” The justice department’s filing on Monday did not specify the reason for the dismissal, saying all parties agreed for the case to be dropped. Prosecutors’ motion called for the case to be fully dismissed “with prejudice” by the end of August, meaning charges could not be brought again, a major victory for Huerta and his lawyers. Ciaran McEvoy, a spokesperson for the US attorney in LA, defended the prosecution in a statement, saying: “The Department of Justice does not arrest people for peacefully protesting.” McEvoy said the department had reached an agreement with Huerta stipulating that if he continued to comply with the terms of his pre-trial release, the case would be entirely dropped. McEvoy also said Huerta had “agreed to accept responsibility for his actions”, though no agreement has been filed in the case, and the justice department spokesperson did not respond to requests for a copy of any agreement. Huerta did not accept responsibility for any criminal activity in his statement to reporters, which decried Trump’s “weaponization of the judicial system”. Huerta’s lawyers, Abbe David Lowell and Marilyn Bednarski, said in a statement that he had been arrested for “peacefully protesting” and exercising his first amendment rights: “This case, like others, sought to silence criticism of the administration’s improper immigration actions. Today’s filing is proof that David and other critics will not be silenced. “This case revealed that the Department of Justice was willing to charge a labor leader with a crime, hold it over him for months, and then walk away from it once the charge couldn’t survive scrutiny,” the lawyers said. “That is not how a justice system is supposed to work.”

title: Savannah Guthrie renews plea for answers in mother’s disappearance: ‘Do the right thing’
summary: Today show host says her family ‘will always ache for’ mother Nancy, who has been missing for nearly six months
body: Savannah Guthrie has posted a new video asking those responsible for her mother’s unsolved disappearance to “do the right thing” and point her family to their matriarch’s location after nearly six months. In a new Instagram video posted on Monday, captioned “Bring her home” alongside a yellow heart emoji, the NBC Today host issued an emotional public plea, saying: “It has been months since our mom was taken from us. Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part. We will never stop looking for her.” She continued: “We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts. The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place, and I know that you have tried to do things the right way. So I’m asking you, begging you, to do the right thing now. “Make the right choice. Help us find her. Tell us where to look for her.” Guthrie went on to say: “I truly believe it is never too late to do the right thing. Help us bring this situation to an end. For all of us, no matter where we’ve been and what we’ve done, I believe there is always a way home. Please make the right choice.” Nancy Guthrie, 84, was reported missing from her home in Tucson, Arizona, on 1 February. Authorities believe she was abducted. Alongside drops of blood discovered on Guthrie’s porch, investigators also recovered DNA from a glove found 2 miles from her home. The glove appeared to resemble one worn by a suspect seen in surveillance footage from the night of her disappearance. However, the glove was later discredited after it was discovered to have belonged to a restaurant worker, not the abductor involved in the case. Savannah Guthrie has used her platform as a host of a national television show to raise awareness about her mother’s disappearance, frequently sharing updates and appeals for information. Her family has also offered a $1m reward for any information leading to their mother being found. Savannah Guthrie in June posted an Instagram story featuring a painting of Jesus Christ and the words: “Oh my, my soul it cries out, soul, it cries out.” Guthrie in March had detailed the agony of not knowing where her mother is, telling her former co-host Hoda Kotb in a tearful interview: “Someone needs to do the right thing. We are in agony. We are in agony. It is unbearable.” The FBI, which has put up an additional $100,000 reward for conclusive information about Nancy Guthrie, is looking for a man approximately 5ft 9in to 5ft 10in tall with an average build. No arrests had been made as of Monday.

title: Burnham’s Ukraine gambit is a symbolic start for PM who wants to look inward
summary: New prime minister wants to focus at home, but his first week already suggests the world has other plans
body: It took just seven days in office for Andy Burnham to meet his first world leader. As he welcomed Volodymyr Zelenskyy to a naval base in Portsmouth on Monday, the new prime minister told the Ukrainian president it was “no accident” he was his first international visitor since entering No 10. “It is intended to send a very clear message,” Burnham told him. “We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.” In short, the UK’s support for Kyiv would continue despite the change in leadership. For Keir Starmer, the relationship with Zelenskyy became one of the defining ones of his premiership. He visited Ukraine four times over his two years in office, inviting the Ukrainian president back to the UK on another four occasions. They also met regularly at international summits. In a symbolic move, Starmer travelled to Ukraine during his final week in office, receiving the order of freedom medal for his role leading the coalition of the willing and helping to persuade Donald Trump back to the table on Ukraine after he flirted with siding with Putin. But over the course of his premiership, the former Labour leader faced accusations of spending too much time on international issues instead of domestic ones, with his critics nicknaming him “never here Keir” and even his own Downing Street team complaining that he “needs to get off a plane”. Burnham, in contrast, has always been clear he would prioritise what was happening at home, reflecting his own political instincts as well as his wariness of not falling into the same trap as his predecessor. But it led some in the Labour party to worry that he would be unprepared for the global stage. “It’s a frustrating characterisation because not many incoming prime ministers, including Keir, have any experience of international affairs,” one of his inner circle said. “Andy has said that his priority will be domestic, but of course there will be moments where he’ll need to be more outward facing.” Day to day, Burnham’s allies have suggested that he will rely on delegating responsibility to his team – including his foreign secretary in Ed Miliband and senior diplomatic adviser in Jonathan Powell, whom he persuaded to stay on in No 10 from the Starmer administration. Labour MPs point out that Yvette Cooper, Miliband’s predecessor, was often left fighting for influence as there were so many other senior figures who saw themselves as the de facto foreign secretary, including the deputy prime minister, David Lammy, Powell, and Starmer himself. One senior MP said: “I suspect that Ed may be in a fortunate position where he is actually given more freedom than other foreign secretaries in the past. As long as Ed is known to have the authority of the PM and to be trusted to speak for him, then this may be his moment.” Other Labour figures suggested that strong prime ministers should be able to delegate and rely on their teams. One said: “I don’t think Andy is particularly interested in foreign affairs. He’ll need to front some things up, but as long as he’s well briefed and charming, he doesn’t need to make the day-to-day decisions like Keir did.” But they warned there would inevitably be moments where complex international issues “crash land” on UK domestic policy – as Starmer found to his cost when dealing with Trump – and he would have no choice but to intervene. Burnham has already indicated he will not shy away from standing up to the US president. “Obviously, the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything that they say,” he told the Guardian last month. There are some with experience of foreign affairs in government who believe that Starmer has already done the hard yards on foreign policy – on Ukraine, the European Union and the US in particular – so Burnham just has to stick to the same course. In his final interview in office, Starmer told his successor that he should not spend less time focusing on international affairs, in order to prioritise the situation at home. “It’s not sensible to think you can just separate these two things out,” he said. “If you’re PM and you care what bills are going to be like in any household around the country, you have to care about finding a lasting solution to the situation in Ukraine, you have to care about what happens in the strait of Hormuz.” But those around Burnham believe he can better balance them. At least for now. They have been watching events in Iran closely, mindful of the potential to cause yet more global economic upheaval should Trump take further action. “Andy has a bit of space now to prioritise policy at home – but it could all be blown off course by Iran,” one Foreign Office insider said. “He has to seize this moment to talk about the domestic, because this window might not come again.”

title: Mitch McConnell still not cleared to resume Senate duties, office says
summary: Kentucky senator has been absent and not seen in public since mid-June after he was hospitalized due to a fall
body: US senator Mitch McConnell is still not cleared to return to work, his office confirmed on Monday, six weeks after he was hospitalized after a fall at his home. An update released alongside a new photograph of the Republican lawmaker – one of the highest-profile figures in Congress, as a former Senate majority leader – said he was undergoing “intense physical therapy” and is “working hard” to get back to his duties. “I’m still working hard to get back to my full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky, keeping up with intense physical therapy per my doctors’ orders,” McConnell, of Kentucky, said in a statement released by his office on Monday. In the statement, he said that he wouldn’t be able to make it to Kentucky this coming weekend for an annual Fancy Farm picnic. “There’s no place I’d rather be on the first Saturday in August than with the good people of western Kentucky, feasting on pork and mutton,” said McConnell, 84. “I hate that I’ll miss the fun this year, but I’m sending my best wishes to the St Jerome community for a successful picnic,” he said. “As always, I appreciate all of your continued well wishes, and I’m looking forward to getting back to the Senate and to Kentucky soon.” McConnell has been absent from the Senate and not seen in public since mid-June, when his office said he was hospitalized and recovering, but did not elaborate on his condition. After weeks of silence, and mounting speculation about his health, McConnell’s office provided an update on 12 July, where they said that he was recovering at a rehabilitation center after having been admitted to the hospital on 14 June after suffering a fall at his home that left him “briefly unconscious”. In the 12 July statement, the senator also disclosed that he had also been dealing with “a mild case of pneumonia” and explained the long silence about his condition by saying that “folks of my generation often hesitate to share the vulnerability that comes with growing older”. McConnell has missed 38 Senate votes since he was hospitalized. He said last year that he would not seek re-election, and is set to retire from the Senate at the end of his term, in January. McConnell’s office also released an image of the senator with his wife, Elaine Chao, which the caption states was from 26 July. Along with the statement and photograph, McConnell’s office also released a statement from the office of the attending physician (OAP) in US Congress. “OAP physicians visit with the Senator every day, discussing all aspects of his rehabilitation care,” the OAP statement said. “Since his discharge from hospital care, he has maintained a strenuous course of physical therapy and rehabilitation, including multiple sessions a day designed to rebuild strength and reduce the risk of future falls.” “His bout with childhood polio continues to be a significant factor in his mobility,” it added. “He is not yet medically cleared to leave the rehab facility and return to the office.”

title: Oil prices fall as US pauses strikes on Iran over strait of Hormuz
summary: Brent crude drops 9% to below $88 a barrel, prompting UK government bond yields to fall
body: Oil prices have dropped sharply as traders bet that a pause in US attacks on Iran could prevent an escalation in the conflict that would further restrict global supply. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, initially fell 9% to below $88 a barrel on Monday after climbing to $100 last week, when the Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea. An attempted recovery later in the day was halted by comments from Donald Trump that the US was having “good talks” with Iran, pushing Brent back down about 8%. The retreat from the short-lived return to more than $100 a barrel came as the US and Iran paused hostilities after 13 days of fighting, amid Trump’s comments suggesting that talks to end the conflict had resumed. Iran said it had stopped “retaliatory” attacks after two nights without American missiles, after the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, told journalists on Sunday that Trump had decided to pause the attacks to allow more time for diplomacy. Separate reports claimed that US military officials had told Trump that the bombing campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness and warned of dwindling stocks of munitions. The comments raised hopes that a renewed focus on diplomatic solutions could de-escalate the regional conflict, which since the end of February has disrupted flows of oil and gas from Gulf states via the strait of Hormuz, and in recent weeks has interrupted vessels leaving the Red Sea via the Bab al-Mandab strait, too. However, the brief reprieve from rising oil prices was met with scepticism by some market observers. “We’ve been here multiple times since March,” said Ole Hvalbye, an analyst at SEB Research. “And each rally on a leak has faded as substance failed to materialise.” John Evans, an analyst at PVM, said he expected oil prices would only be able to fall further if there was a meaningful decline in demand, “not questionable mini-ceasefires”. He said: “The market seems to be forever seeking good news from an arena that really is not providing any. A stay of military strikes might seem an improvement, but it does not come with any guarantees that oil will soon flow from the area.” Analysts at Deutsche Bank led by Jim Reid said the 10% increase in Brent crude prices last week had “added to fears that the global economy was facing a prolonged inflation shock, and that the Fed might need to hike rates more aggressively in response”. The expectation of higher inflation caused by rising global energy costs has put pressure on central banks to raise interest rates. In recent weeks that has pushed up sovereign bond yields, which move inversely to prices. However, the oil price drop on Monday prompted yields to fall. The yield on UK 10-year government debt dropped below 5%, down 0.05 percentage points during the day. The rate-sensitive two-year yield fell 0.06 percentage points to 4.35%. Higher oil prices could harm Trump politically, with many members of the Republican party nervous of the effects of inflation on their prospects at midterm elections in November. Some Federal Reserve policymakers may feel the need to raise interest rates to try to counteract price increases, a move that could slow the US economy – despite Trump’s wish for lower rates.

title: Cracker Barrel CEO to step down after overseeing logo backlash last year
summary: Julie Masino faced criticism as restaurant chain was called ‘woke’ and ‘soulless’ after unveiling modernized logo
body: Cracker Barrel’s CEO, Julie Masino, is stepping down, the restaurant announced on Monday, nearly a year after the company was swept into a political maelstrom over proposed modernizations to its branding. Critics on social media denounced the Tennessee-based rustic restaurant chain as “woke” as well as “sterile and soulless” after it unveiled an updated logo that removed Uncle Herschel, the overall-clad man leaning against a barrel in the restaurant’s original logo, last August. Donald Trump weighed in on the updates soon after, posting: “WTF is wrong with Cracker Barrel?!” and demanding on social media that the company “admit a mistake”. The company announced that it would revert back to its old logo soon after the social media reaction exploded. Masino, who has served as the chain’s CEO since 2023, told the rightwing commentator Glenn Beck in December that she felt “fired by America” after the controversy. Cracker Barrel’s stock dropped nearly 3% after the announcement of Masino’s departure. The chain’s new CEO, David Deno, will take over on 10 August, and Masino will remain until October to help with the transition. “Cracker Barrel is a truly iconic American brand, defined by its unique combination of warm country hospitality, timeless appeal, and deep connection with guests across generations,” Deno said in a statement. Masino’s departure the latest fallout from social media-fueled backlash against brands accused of appealing to certain political ideals. The Harris Poll found last year that a quarter of Americans have changed their shopping habits to align with their morals, with 50% of Democrats and 41% of Republicans responding that they stopped shopping at stores opposing their political views. Some companies have quickly felt the financial strain of these calls to action. In 2023, after Target announced a pride month collection and Bud Light aired an advertisement with a transgender influencer, both companies announced declines in sales. On the other side of the political aisle, Target was pulled as a sponsor from Minneapolis’s annual pride festival last year after it announced it was ending its diversity, equality and inclusion policies. Not all of these boycotts have been successful, though – Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey saw great success at its global box office debut, despite Elon Musk and other critics castigating the movie’s cast as part of a “woke” agenda. Cracker Barrel has had a history of discriminatory treatment against diners and staff. In 1991, the chain blocked the hiring of LGBTQ+ workers and dismissed 11 staff members, though it later backed down from that policy. In 2004, Cracker Barrel paid $8.7m to settle discrimination allegations from Black customers who said they were denied service and Black employees who said they received more “back of house” assignments compared with their white counterparts.
